sections.history: Thiruchitrakoodam is not a separate temple but a shrine of Vishnu within the Thillai Nataraja temple complex at Chidambaram, and it is one of the 108 Divya Desams — the abodes of Vishnu sung by the Alvar saints in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham — in Chola Nadu. Kulasekhara Alvar and Thirumangai Alvar offered their mangalasasanam here. One temple-history source attributes the installation of the image to the Pallava king Nandivarman, in the eighth century. Tradition adds that in the twelfth century, under Kulothunga Chola II, the image was removed and its festival image carried to Tirupati, where Govindaraja is still worshipped; the shrine was reinstated in the mid-sixteenth century under Krishnappa Nayak. The present structure is largely of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, with later additions, though sources differ.
sections.architecture: The shrine stands inside the precincts of the Nataraja temple, in the Dravidian manner, with Govindaraja Perumal reclining in the sanctum and the Goddess Pundarikavalli Thayar enshrined separately. The temple tank is known as the Pundarika Pushkarini. Much of the fabric is of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, with later additions, in keeping with the style of the surrounding complex.
sections.legends: Tradition says Govindaraja reclines facing the shrine of Nataraja, for he is held to have witnessed — and judged — the dance contest between Shiva and Parvati. The verses of Kulasekhara Alvar on Thillai Chitrakoodam are remembered for recounting the story of Rama, so that the shrine holds a place in the Vaishnava memory of the Ramayana as well as in Shaiva Chidambaram.
sections.festivals: The best-known observance is the ten-day Chithirai Vasantha Utsavam, held in April–May. The festival of Gajendra Moksham, recalling the elephant freed by Vishnu, is also kept. Vaikunta Ekadashi and the days of the Alvars follow the wider Vaishnava calendar. Dates follow the Tamil calendar, so confirm them locally.
sections.experience: Visitors come for the Nataraja temple and find here a quiet Vishnu shrine in the same precincts — a rare meeting of Shaiva and Vaishnava devotion. Look for the reclining lord turned toward Nataraja, and ask the priests about the Pundarika Pushkarini and local darshan arrangements.

visit.timings: Open daily with morning and evening darshan sessions and a midday closure; confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear removed before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is restricted in and around the sanctum; follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.gettingThere: The shrine lies inside the Thillai Nataraja temple complex in Chidambaram, which is on the Chennai–Thanjavur rail line, about 230 km south of Chennai, with regular trains and buses. Puducherry, roughly 65 km north, is the most convenient airport.
